item.title: Grasim Industries Q2FY27 results: Net profit jumps to ₹2,306 crore
item.description: The Aditya Birla Group flagship's standalone net profit jumped to ₹2,306 crore ($244.93 million) for the quarter ended September 30, from ₹805 crore a year earlier ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: India's Grasim Industries reported a second-quarter profit that nearly tripled on Friday, boosted by dividend income from its cement-making company UltraTech Cement.The Aditya Birla Group flagship's standalone net profit jumped to ₹2,306 crore ($244.93 million) for the quarter ended September 30, from ₹805 crore a year earlier.The company received dividend income worth ₹3,968 crore from UltraTech Cement, which boosted its operating profit by 158% on-year to ₹4,615 crore.Meanwhile, its fibre business reported an 29% year-on-year rise in revenue, further aiding profit.The fibre business continued to benefit from higher prices which helped boost margins, while narrowing losses at its paints and business-to-business e-commerce ventures also aided profit.Grasim's newer Birla Opus paints business reported 35% growth in revenue to ₹1,337 crore, as the company continued to expand in a market long dominated by competitors Asian Paints and Berger Paints.Sandalone revenue from operations surged nearly 33% to ₹12,747 crore in the quarter.The company incurred a one-time impairment charge worth ₹825 crore during the quarter related a its joint venture.Excluding the charge, profit more than tripled to ₹3,765 crore.

item.title: Jindal Power secures $470 million loan for Botswana power project
item.description: A group of three Indian lenders - Axis Bank, ICICI Bank and Export-Import Bank of India - provided the nine-year door-to-door facility to Jindal Power ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Saikat Das The power arm of Jindal Group has signed an offshore loan of about $470 million to help fund a power project in Botswana, according to people familiar with the matter, as one of India’s largest conglomerates boosts its footprint in the African nation. A group of three Indian lenders — Axis Bank Ltd., ICICI Bank Ltd. and Export-Import Bank of India — provided the nine-year door-to-door facility to Jindal Power Ltd., the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. The loan is being syndicated with some global institutional lenders expected to join, the people said. The financing highlights the growing overseas ambitions of Indian energy companies as they pursue opportunities in markets where rising electricity demand is driving investment in generation and transmission infrastructure. Jindal Power raised about $500 million in an earlier round of financing in February meant for its expansion abroad. Jindal Power built a 700-megawatt coal power plant in Botswana that is scheduled for commissioning next month, according to its website. Mining operations in the Southern African nation are big electricity consumers and Botswana has been hoping to use its coal resources, estimated at more than 200 billion tonnes, to build a petroleum fuels industry to reduce its reliance on imports from South Africa and Namibia. Botswana owns 15% of the world’s biggest diamond miner, De Beers. The loan facility is priced at about 300 to 325 basis points over the benchmark Secured Overnight Financing Rate, the people said. The borrowing cost is expected to decline after the project is commissioned, they added. Representatives from Jindal Power, Axis Bank, ICICI Bank and the Export-Import Bank of India did not reply to requests seeking comment. Indian borrowers have raised $24.2 billion through foreign-currency loans so far this year, about 8% lower from a year ago, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, as elevated hedging costs have deterred some companies from tapping overseas debt markets.  Jindal Power, however, benefits from a natural hedge because the African project’s revenues are expected to be denominated in, or linked to, foreign currency, reducing its exposure to exchange-rate swings.

item.title: US lawmakers push for tougher curbs on advanced AI chip exports to China

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US lawmakers push for tougher curbs on advanced AI chip exports to China

US lawmakers push for tougher curbs on advanced AI chip exports to China US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Huang

The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China | Image: Bloomberg

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 1:30 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Chinese AI shares tumbled on Friday, as investors worried that Jensen Huang's departure as Nvidia CEO could further restrict Chinese access to advanced US chips, deepening the technology divide between the world's two biggest economies.   US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Huang, who has pushed to preserve access to the Chinese market and has close ties with US President Donald Trump.   Huang stepped down after news reports of a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China's surging AI development.   Senior White House officials were also discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington. Also Read

Alice Huang had stake in China data centre serving Huawei, says report

From gaming chips to AI dominance: How Nvidia became a tech powerhouse

Fallout from Nvidia scandal may dampen investor exuberance around AI boom

US lawmakers step up pressure on Howard Lutnick as Nvidia row deepens

Meet Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim CEO after Jensen Huang's exit

A growing number of lawmakers have criticized Lutnick for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a US trade blacklist, and questioned whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China.   Nvidia's advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China's access to Nvidia's chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

"The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here," Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favored limiting China's access to the advanced technology. "I think there's a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take."   Investors dumped shares in Chinese AI models and hardware suppliers to the US on Friday, with AI model stocks Z.AI and MiniMax Group tumbling 12% and 8.4% respectively.   Data center suppliers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology, whose businesses are heavily reliant on US markets, also slumped more than 8%.   The Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

REPUBLICANS EYE EXPORT RESTRICTIONS   The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.   Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company's chips remotely.   Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense  authorization bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.   The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access Nvidia chips.  SCRUTINY OF HUANG LIKELY TO CONTINUE   Huang's resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.

"Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang," Cheung said.   Cheung said Huang's departure could weaken Nvidia's influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports. He said Nvidia's new leadership could also reconsider the company's China strategy as it seeks to rebuild trust with US policymakers.   Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for his testimony.

Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang.

item.title: Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams for hours, hits users globally
item.description: More than 130,000 users reported Outlook access issues on Downdetector, while thousands faced problems with Teams and Copilot ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams for hours, hits users globally

Microsoft outage disrupts Outlook, Teams for hours, hits users globally In its latest update, Microsoft said efforts to improve serviceability were not progressing as expected

At its peak, Downdetector showed more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems in the US around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday (Photo: Reuters)

Reuters Chicago 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 7:45 AM IST

Listen to This Article

A disruption of Microsoft services such as Outlook, Teams and Copilot stretched into Asia-Pacific business hours on Friday after affecting thousands of US users, as the tech giant struggled to fix server problems it blamed for the outage. The outage hit government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States, as well as companies including OpenAI and Anthropic. It is the second disruption to Microsoft's 365 services this year, raising concerns that repeated failures could push corporate clients to question Microsoft's reliability. In its latest update, Microsoft said it had applied adjustments to the affected servers, but they did not result in sustained recovery. It said it had observed some partial recovery in the regions where it applied the adjustments.

"We're reviewing what additional actions we can take to improve overall infrastructure stability," the company said on X. Downdetector, which tracks outages by collating status reports from a number of sources, showed more than 18,000 reports of Outlook problems in the US at 11:30 p.m. ET (0430 GMT). It also showed outages for several Microsoft services in the Asia-Pacific region, including India, Australia and Japan, early Friday local time. Also Read

Microsoft 365 outage continues as company sees limited recovery in services

Microsoft presses Trump admin to scuttle ban on Chinese data center tech

Microsoft's $25 billion blowout bond puts it in AI winners' circle

Big tech's $750 billion AI bet faces strain with slowing core growth

Microsoft's cloud growth, cash flow offer respite from AI spending fears

At its peak, Downdetector showed more than 130,000 reports of Outlook problems in the US around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday. The outage has lasted for about 12 hours. In a service health notice, Microsoft said features of Microsoft 365 services that depended on Exchange Online and email were affected, while elements that did not rely on Exchange Online remained functional. Exchange Online is the company's cloud-based messaging platform that delivers email, calendar, contacts, and tasks.

The company added that it was "not aware" of any malicious activity that was causing the outage. IMPACT ON EMAIL SYSTEMS Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said that Microsoft believed it was not dealing with a cyberattack. "They believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke said at a press conference. "The impact that they are dealing with ... is very much on email systems," the minister added. Australia's spy agency and federal police were among organizations caught up in the outage on Friday.

The CrowdStrike malfunction of 2024 was one of the largest internet disruptions, hobbling technology systems in hospitals, banks, and airports, highlighting the vulnerability of the world's interconnected technologies. The US House of Representatives said the outage impacted its users and its engineers were working with Microsoft. Japanese Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters that the outage was affecting the government's information system infrastructure. BUSINESSES FEEL THE IMPACT US AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic said they had faced issues with Microsoft connectors, while Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were impacted. The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as cancelling a bond repurchase agreement transaction it had already scheduled, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters, declining to provide the name of the company.

Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro, said investors would likely look past the outage but that repeated disruptions could hurt Microsoft over time. "I think investors will take this in their stride for now, because very few of these customers can realistically walk away from the Microsoft ecosystem overnight," Gilbert said. "The bigger worry is that this isn't the first 365 outage this year, and if reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider's hands. The market will want to see Microsoft prove it can keep the lights on before it asks customers to spend more on Copilot."

Microsoft faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and also in October last year. Microsoft last month reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software, and a range of industries worldwide. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on November 12, rescheduled it to November 16 citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.
